summary: Stone light of 1816 on the tip of Great Island at the entrance to Hyannis Harbor; the Board's 1857 recommendation ended it in 1858. Private island, not open.

structures.note: rubblestone per the archive; conical; stone tower still standing (LighthouseFriends); about 21 m at first lighting; a brick superstructure had been added by the 1843 survey, making the entire height 25 feet (New England Lighthouses quoting Lewis 1843)
one and a half storeys, 16 by 30 feet (New England Lighthouses); dismantled in 1930s, the stones used for a new house on the island

staffing.note: two keepers, both Peaks, from 1816 to 1858

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The archive gives 1855 as the year discontinued. LighthouseFriends and New England Lighthouses give 1858: the Board recommended discontinuance in 1857, and the light ended when Bishop and Clerks first shone on 1 October 1858. LighthouseFriends says a lightship was stationed offshore for a short time from 1855; neither secondary source explains the archive's 1855 date. The story uses 1858.

notes_for_editor: Every source for this station is secondary: LighthouseFriends and New England Lighthouses both draw on Light-House Board reports (1838, 1843, 1857, 1865) that the local corpus does not hold (its lhb series starts in 1891). Their quotations of those reports are cited to the secondary page, and the story uses them only as quoted. The archive's place record has a private owner, no coordinates (0,0), and 'Year Discontinued: 1855', which conflicts with the other two sources; the archive also lists two men as Contractor with no dates, and the sources read do not say what they did. The USLHS place match was by name and 'Point Gammon' only; the tool warned that its coordinates were far from the station (the record's coordinates are at Great Island, which both secondary sources place). The location matches the station record and both secondary sources. The record's events list has both 1855 and 1858 as deactivation dates; the story uses 1858. The private family who owns Great Island and converted the tower is not named in the story (the 1970s conversion is attributed to a family member), since the guide asks us not to name private residents of a converted lighthouse. Malcolm G. Chace and Charles Barney Cory are named as historical owners. No photos proposed.
